I would also like to mention the hospital's kitchen: breakfasts, lunches, dinners, and snacks - always on time. The food is quite tasty and caloric. The patient rooms are cleaned wet 1-2 times a day, and there are flowers on the windowsills.

Good afternoon to all! On March 7, I went to the hospital to have a conization of cervical cysts done, it was my first time without a prior appointment with the doctors. I sat in the reception area for 2 hours with the girls who had come for their own issues, we were all freezing, but the worst was yet to come. After the paperwork was done, I was given some clothes and told the room number, I waited. At 11 am, I was called to the operating room, I went in on edge and asked if there was an alternative to anesthesia, as my body doesn't tolerate it well. I was met with a barrage of abuse, I was called a spoiled woman and told I should have gone to a private clinic. A man, who was either Jewish or not Russian, was recording everything and making comments about me having two children and being afraid of anesthesia. I started crying uncontrollably. Things only got worse from there. I woke up in the ward at 12:30, feeling freezing cold in just a gown. I managed to cover myself with a blanket and looked at the time. I had been lying there half-naked for an hour and a half. A girl who had been admitted with me was brought in. She asked how I was, I mumbled something, and she told me I had been unconscious in the corridor for 10 minutes before being brought to the ward. I managed to call my husband. I felt nauseous several times and had to crawl to the sink. I felt so bad that everything was spinning. My husband came to pick me up at 5 pm, but no one had checked on me during that time. I felt like a abandoned dog. I understand that it's hard to get hold of anyone before a holiday, but anesthesia is no joke. I got up, got dressed, and wanted some tea. I went to the canteen, but the girls eating there were rude and said there were no cups, I had to bring my own. I managed to get to the elevator, a woman came and we went down together. I got dressed, went out, sat in the car, and cried from helplessness and horror at what had happened. I've never encountered such cruel treatment anywhere else. To lie there for 11 hours until 5 pm without anyone asking how I was feeling. Now I understand why people say: "If you want to die, welcome to the first hospital.

opinion_term: shouted at the top of his voice
english_translated:
Hello, dear patients, your relatives and friends who have been in the Central Clinical Hospital of the Russian Academy of Sciences at the address of Litovsky Boulevard. I want to share our sad story with you. Maybe it's just our story, but maybe this information will be useful to someone. And I just want to get it all out of my soul. I couldn't tell this for about two years, but today something prompted me to take the iPad and write it all down. It all started with the fact that my father, a doctor of geophysical sciences, was diagnosed with rectal cancer. During the examination in this hospital, which is free for him, the doctors insisted on surgery. Father agreed. I came with him to the doctors who were supposed to perform the operation. Their names are Azimov Rustam Hasanovich and Volobuev Andrey Vladimirovich. Listening to the advice of my friends and acquaintances, I asked how much it would cost. In response, I received almost indignant: "What are you talking about, it's free for your father. You just need to go there and buy this equipment." And this is in the leading hospital of Moscow!
Well, I went. Paid about twenty thousand or more. Brought it to the doctors. They appointed the day of the operation. Everything seemed fine. During the operation, I was sitting in the corridor. I saw a strange picture - another doctor ran out of the doctor's office with our equipment. And this at the end of the operation! Did they forget to take it!? After the anesthesia wore off, Dad felt okay at first. In my naivety, I brought Dr. Azimov a bottle of good whiskey. (From the bottom of my heart). I handed him the bottle, and then Azimov shouted at the top of his voice: "What am I, a plumber, that you're giving me a bottle!" I was in shock. He shouted loudly, for the whole corridor to hear. It was like I was burned! What should I do!? After that, they told me that I needed to give money. But this hospital is free for my father! And we bought the equipment! Several feelings were raging in my soul. Dislike for Azimov, the feeling that they were blackmailing me with my father's life and death, and thoughts of how much money they wanted. I gave them ten thousand. Put it in his pocket. Lord, even now it's unpleasant to remember! No, it's not about the money! Of course not! But this disgusting, contemptible hypocrisy! But after the first operation, Dad felt bad, and they performed another one on him, who is 75 years old! What happened there, we don't know. Father, already afraid for his life, insisted that I give more money to these "doctors." Azimov took the money with a look like he was finally getting his debt paid. He gave me his phone number, and we had to communicate with him by phone. He consulted us arrogantly, pretending to be extremely busy. After the operation, my father felt bad all the time, and then metastases started. I want to address Azimov. Of course, it's impossible to prove that you behaved like this, it's impossible to prove that you took the money (and this is a criminal offense). I didn't record it on my phone, I was thinking about Dad. But there is God, and God sees everything! And everyone in this life gets what they deserve! I don't hate you, Rustam (I did before). I know that you will get what you deserve in your life. I pity you. Maybe it would be better for you to learn to be a plumber.
Friends! I repeat that this is just our story. And this is just a cry from my soul. You make your own conclusions. I sincerely wish you health! Some doctors really need it!

I don't know why this hospital is considered good. It hasn't been for a long time. There's no funding. If you don't believe me, there's a luxurious new building next to the neurosurgery ward that has been standing idle for many years, and expensive equipment is rotting in the basement because there's no money to finish the building and put it into use.
My father was in the hospital under SOGAZ insurance, we were transferred from the Central Clinical Hospital with a terrifying diagnosis of brain cancer, an urgent operation was needed, at the end of December 2012.
Without money, no one will even approach you, and what's worse, they won't approach you even with money. My father had a neurosurgical operation, they removed the brain cancer tumor. The operation went very well, the surgeon, Miklashovich Eduard Richardovich, is a professional from God, the next day after the operation, they took my father out of intensive care, he was talking, completely lucid. But then, the New Year holidays came. And instead of improvement, my father almost died.
There was no one left in the hospital. They didn't give me the doctors' mobile phone numbers, I was sitting with my father alone, the nurses only came to give injections twice a day. No amount of money could make them work. Once, before leaving for the night, I left them a bottle of Italian champagne for 2000 rubles, good chocolate candies, and 1000 rubles in cash, so they would come to him at night, because after the operation, he had insomnia and nightmares. My father, always a strong and tough man, cried from fear like a child, they locked him in a stuffy room so he wouldn't disturb the nurses, and took away the nurse call button, hid it behind the bed, he couldn't reach it, I paid for a private room with a TV, but they were too lazy to even turn it on for him! And he lay there in the heat, in the dark, for hours without sleep, motionless, because he had paralysis on the entire right side! In short, out of the 4 on-duty nurses, 2 were normal, but two were just sadists. I did their job, sat with my father from 10 am to 10 pm, and drove home every day for 55 km (I live in Lyubertsy). So, when I wasn't there, they didn't even always change his diaper and feed him! Although I always left 500 rubles every evening before leaving, so they would look after him! In Moscow, this is a normal price for a caregiver, but in this hospital, the sisters don't consider money!
The doctors in the hospital are not much better. During the holidays, there were only 3 patients left on the floor, who were probably so heavy that they couldn't be discharged. The doctors DIDN'T COME THEMSELVES! I had to catch them for hours, drag them into the room. Despite the fact that I gave everyone money and expensive cognac before the operation, and then some more. And my father was a commercial patient, the insurance company paid huge sums for us. I encountered such a state of the patient for the first time, I'm not a doctor, I didn't know what to do with a bedridden patient. And no one told me how to take care of him. No one even advised me to do something urgently or hire a professional for money. Although, the LFK specialist and massage should have been provided to us for free by the insurance! But the massage was only after the New Year holidays, around January 10th, and the LFK specialist said he would only work for cash, because, you see, he doesn't get anything from the money that the insurance company pays by wire, it all goes to the administration. I tried to argue and say that I'm not an oligarch either, and that if the insurance is paying, then I'm not obliged to, but he was inflexible. I had to pay so he would put my father on his feet and teach him to walk again with paralysis in his leg.
But that was later, and at first, I watched my father's condition worsen every day. After a week of lying like that, he could barely talk, he was almost motionless. I ran around the floors, looking for the on-duty doctors, begging them to come, but they ignored me or came just for show. And only one kind doctor, unfortunately, I don't know his last name, with a Korean appearance, said that, actually, the patient should have been sitting on the bed from the 3rd day after the operation, taught me how to do it, fixing it with a chair, - and also taught me how to do various procedures to prevent lung stasis.
I did everything myself, it was very hard. Some nurses helped me change the dirty, wet sheets and diapers under my father, some wrinkled their noses in disgust and refused to help.
And most importantly, in the end, when the cancer diagnosis was officially confirmed (histology, biopsy) - according to the insurance contract, they were no longer supposed to pay for further treatment. And they discharged us from the hospital. A bedridden patient who could barely take a few steps down the corridor with the help of a specialist. I begged, pleaded not to discharge him, there should be some recovery, procedures, rehabilitation. I was ready to pay for further stay myself. But no, they threw us out. They didn't provide an ambulance or anything. I had to hire porters, they carried my father into the house on their hands because our house has 2 floors without an elevator.
You know, this is a terrible hospital, terrible treatment of patients. Even with money, you're not considered a person there.

I endured it because I needed his conclusion to be hospitalized. After paying another 2500 and waiting another hour, I finally entered Meshalkina's office, but she said she didn't know where I had been and that her workday was over, and I had to wait for the next on-duty doctor. Doctor Siluyanova conducted an examination, although she couldn't establish a diagnosis this way, wrote in my medical record for a long time, and said that the abortion would cost 50-60 thousand rubles, but there's no guarantee they would accept me. She needs to convene a consultation, and the chief doctor has a scientific council, and I have to wait a few more hours until it's over. In the end, I spent from 8 am to 5 pm in this so-called hospital, paying for unnecessary tests, going through humiliation and stress, and received a refusal over the phone! This is fraud. People, be vigilant if you want to preserve your health and honestly earned money. I filed a complaint with the prosecutor's office.

**Wow, the head nurse!**

Hello, I want to share my emotions after staying at this hospital. I've never written a review before and haven't read them either, but I really wanted to do this. I've never encountered such treatment in our country.

I was admitted with my child to the 5th department with a diagnosis of lacunar angina, fever, etc. We were received warmly and treatment began, but my child refused to stay in the ward and I had to sit on a bench in the corridor near the head nurse's office, watching the department's work. Well, what can I say, at first glance, a fragile girl with a friendly smile, but she's quite tough, my child even gave her the nickname "Cinderella").

First, she writes something down, then she takes the child to the toilet on a stretcher, five minutes later she's holding the child in the ward while the mother runs to the toilet, ten minutes later she returns with a basket full of medicines, and all you can hear throughout the department is "Nastya", then from another end: "Where's our Nastya?" And she's already standing at the door, still with that smile - amazing speed! And despite all this, she finds time to ask what's wrong, she came up to us and said we're not supposed to be in the corridor, she asked if there's a conflict in the ward, if something happened, I explained why I couldn't stay, and Anastasia Valerievna, joked with my child, gave us masks, and my daughter went to the ward herself half an hour later.

Everyone says head nurses are mean, but I want to say that I've proven this wrong myself, here the head nurse works day and night shifts and still remains friendly and interested. A real person!

It's very hard to be in the hospital when you're a man and there are only women around, but when you feel that there are people who will ask, who will be interested, it becomes easier. Health to you and your loved ones, Kobleva Anastasia Valerievna.

And of course, to the head of the department Mitrofanova I.V. and doctor Shakarayan A.K. - competent people, it's nice to know that there are still doctors by the grace of God! You, nurses and orderlies - thank you! A wonderful team!

Thank you, the leader, for having such a humane staff!

I had been dreaming of a beautiful chest for several years. After fluctuations in weight and the last 5 years of intense sports, there was little left of my chest.
This year, I finally decided on mammoplasty. Like many others, I thoroughly studied the information on the internet, reading reviews and studying possible complications.
I live in two cities, Omsk and Moscow. Initially, I wanted to have this operation done in Omsk and visited a huge number of surgeons, and had already chosen a doctor to whom I was registered. The approximate date was set for 2 months later, as I needed to fly to Moscow.
Upon arrival, I saw an advertisement for SanLasar with the note "Promotion! Breast augmentation for 65,000 plus a compression bra as a gift." I initially thought that the implants and dressings were not included in this operation, but the price was still very low. I had no initial thoughts of having this operation done for such money, but out of curiosity, I called the clinic. To my surprise, I learned that only the tests were not included in this price. Deciding that this was even more suspicious, I tried to dismiss the idea from my head.
The duration of my stay in Moscow was increasing, and I no longer knew when I would be able to go to Omsk (due to work). And then I remembered SanLasar again. This time, I actively studied the reviews of the clinic and the reviews of the surgeons. In the process of searching, I found the page of Dr. Blinov D.A. on Instagram, found patients, and asked "Are they satisfied with the result?" I received an answer that they were simply happy. I also liked the photos of the work, and I decided to have a consultation.
After the consultation, my doubts disappeared, and I was already sure that I would be operated on by this surgeon.
On the appointed day of the operation, I came to the clinic. I was greeted by a friendly and smiling nurse, Tatyana, who showed me my room, and then everything happened quite quickly, and I avoided any unpleasant waiting. Dmitry Alexandrovich made the markings. He also warned me again, after the consultation, that there was asymmetry in the "original" and it might remain. I could see this asymmetry in the mirror: one breast was higher and smaller than the other, plus one nipple was more developed. All the surgeons at the previous consultations also warned me that this defect would most likely not be eliminated. Spoiler alert: when Dmitry Alexandrovich showed me my chest, I was pleasantly surprised that it was even.
And so: anesthesia, operation, I started hearing voices, I felt very cold, and I passed out again. I was freezing terribly, the whole time Tatyana was caring for me, they put an electric blanket on me, I got warmer, and I fell asleep. The state after anesthesia was not very good, and I woke up quite hard. I didn't have any particular pain: I felt terrible pressure and pain in the muscles of my chest.
The next morning, the drains were removed, and I went home.
The first week was difficult, not because of the pain, but because of the weakness and helplessness. Practically every day I experienced new sensations, and they scared me. Dmitry Alexandrovich was always in touch and explained to me what sensations were and why they were happening, gave consultations and monitored my condition. Thanks to this, I felt calmer.
To my surprise, my sensitivity did not disappear, and there was no significant swelling.
Now, a month has passed, and the result has exceeded all my expectations. My chest is already becoming softer, and I am getting used to it, and I don't feel any discomfort.
To everyone who is considering mammoplasty, I can say that the price of the operation is not important, but the professionalism of the surgeon is. The word "to be a plastic surgeon" means a lot in this field. I can confidently recommend Blinov D.A., and I am sure that other patients will support me.

1. Before the operation, a doctor rushed in, saying the operating room was being prepared. He answered my questions reluctantly, backing towards the door, and then rushed out. A minute later, he rushed back in, telling me to undress and follow him to the operating room, without even leaving the room. Naked, in the short gown given by the nurses with a deep V-neck, I rushed after the doctor, while he discussed where to put my slippers and find an anesthesiologist for me. Once on the operating table, I was told to remove my jewelry and other movable items. After the operation, the doctor stopped by to ask about my well-being. When I asked about post-operative care, he referred to the discharge papers, saying everything was written there. Later, I found a scary diagnosis in the discharge papers, in chronic form. After researching the symptoms online, I realized I probably didn't have the disease before the operation, with no signs of the usual gnarly process and severe tube pain. I couldn't confirm the diagnosis or rule out an error because the doctor had already gone home, and other staff referred me to him. Now I have to go through tests to exclude or treat this sentence. I hope the operation was done for a trivial diagnosis I came in with.
2. Accommodation. In the surgical department, two-bed rooms (like boxes) are mostly empty, but I was placed in a box where a man was lying in the next room. The rooms are stuffy, open windows don't help (it's +20 outside), so I have to open the doors.
3. After the anesthesia, I couldn't sleep or even rest. The volume on the TVs in the rooms can't be fixed, as is common in such institutions. My neighbor might have been hard of hearing, as I could hear his TV even at the opposite end of the department. After the (meager) lunch, when it's supposed to be quiet time, the cleaner comes for a planned cleaning. It's like a movie: seeing me asleep, the lady starts loudly complaining about her life, saying she has 21 rooms and not enough time to clean, and other departmental problems bother her greatly. She wiped the window frames, sills, and plinths with one cloth, leaving black streaks on everything. I politely explained that I was recovering from general anesthesia and asked her not to make noise, as I wanted to sleep, but she ignored me. My request offended the hospital worker so much that she started wiping the furniture in the room even harder, which eventually cleaned off the streaks from previous "cleanings." After completing and exceeding the planned workload, the lady started changing the fresh linens on the neighboring unoccupied bed, loudly cursing at me. I should mention that the lady was monologuing, I don't like participating in such battles, and I didn't have the energy to argue.

I still have to clarify if I have this magical diagnosis and heal the bruises on my hands (I look like a drug addict).

01.10.12 I received a quota for my mother's operation at the Institute named after A.V. Vishnevsky, and involuntarily learned the administrative side. After the operation, they keep you for no more than 10 days and discharge you with further treatment of the "raw" stitch at your place of residence. The conveyor is ensured by top-class surgeons of a wide profile. But they are slaves to the administration. My mother with the diagnosis of "abdominal tumors" was placed in the thoracic (lung) department.
The next day after the operation, the patient is brought to the ward (violating the terms of reanimation service, and operations can be different!). My mother on this next day developed brain hypoxia; in such a state, a person does not control themselves - and began to demand discharge, being hung with drainage tubes. The administration and doctors agreed, only the drain will be removed!
I had to insist on my mother's psychiatric examination to prove the doctors' mistake to them. At first, they refused to call an ambulance psychiatric service; lawyers convinced me that this is against the law. Then the professor added that everyone has the right to suicide, so let her be discharged. The ambulance psychiatric service team, arriving, confirmed my words about my mother's condition. In my presence, it was said about the violation of article 26 of the RF Criminal Code*. The arriving doctor strongly recommended that my mother be placed in the reanimation department for further treatment. The administration agreed.
... but she deceived me, explaining that there was no free space in the reanimation department, then strictly said that psychomotor reactions due to hypoxia are a common thing, and soon a discharge was appointed. By this time, my mother's stitch had begun to fester. I insisted on a thorough examination of the stitch, appealing to the human compassion of the doctor (a top-class specialist!). He agreed and ... discovered a purulent wound with the beginning of infection. An emergency repeat operation was performed to clean the abdominal cavity, and then a constant drain of the wound with frequent bandages was appointed. Allergies to most of the prescribed medications. There is no replacement due to a limited list. As a result, almost all of the intestinal microflora was killed. On the eve of discharge, one of the young doctors said in a tone of reproach - don't you know that your mother is lying in the thoracic department?! And what kind of claims can there be here?
Most likely, our case is not the only one in the history of the institute; it's just that there is no information about others. Probably, this incident was needed to stop the concealment of the violation of patients' rights.
*Article 26 of the RF Criminal Code - Crime committed through negligence.
A. A crime committed through negligence is considered an act committed through carelessness or recklessness.
B. A crime is considered committed through recklessness if the person foresaw the possibility of the occurrence of socially dangerous consequences of their actions (inaction), but self-confidently assumed that these consequences would be prevented without sufficient grounds for this.
C. A crime is considered committed through carelessness if the person did not foresee the possibility of the occurrence of socially dangerous consequences of their actions (inaction), although with the necessary caution and foresight, they should have and could have foreseen these consequences.

I want to address Dmitry Anatolyevich. Hello! We have a problem, and it's not small in scale. First, about my family: I have two children, the first is a newborn infant with disabilities, the second is frequently ill. Once, I ended up in the pediatric Izmailovsky Hospital No. 3 in the boxed infectious department (September 15-22), it's been about two and a half months since then. Then I was hospitalized again with my first child in the same hospital in the gastroenterology department. We were there for nine days, and then I received a call on my mobile from the TB dispensary, saying that we had contact with a TB patient in September in the hospital in the boxed department with the service staff. It turned out that the contact was with a person who was distributing food. Now, all TB dispensaries are searching for about 1,500 children, not counting adults. The chief physician of this hospital (Zharkov) refuses to comment on anything, and the deputy for medical affairs refers to the polyclinic, saying that they are blowing up a scandal. But as far as I know, the dispensary does not come home if there is no cause for concern. Now, about what is happening in the hospitals: there should be wards for at least one mother with a child (not 4 mothers and 6 children in a box with different diseases). There should be a toilet and a bathroom, at least at the end of the corridor (mothers have a toilet in the basement, where water drips from the ceiling, and there are no baths, nor beds. Mothers are forced to sit on chairs all night, and you can't lie down next to the child in a small bed, and many spread a diaper on the tile and sleep like that. If the child is three years old, then the parents in the hospital are not fed, they cannot go out, there is only boiling water when the cook wants it, there are no outlets in the ward. The situation is the same in other departments, if there is a bath, it works until 20:00 in the evening, and then a lock is put on it. Medical sisters who should sit constantly on duty are forced to distribute food, not tablets. And the list can go on and on, we keep encountering this reality and it's just sad for RUSSIA, such a great power and such treatment of people! Why is it like this? How to solve ALL these problems without gagging us? How to give birth to children if no one considers themselves guilty when a child is born with disabilities, and everyone persuades you to refuse? HOW TO ACHIEVE JUSTICE????
